title: LIVE: Trump Xi - CEA Crash - Explosion
content:
Welcome to China Insider, my name is —
So this May, there's one event that political observers have been watching very closely: President Trump's visit to China. But what makes this trip so special — and why does it matter so much right now?
Trump-Xi Meeting: 3 Remarkables [ko cần đọc dòng này]
The last time Trump set foot in China was back in 2017 — when he sat in the Forbidden City, eyes closed, watching a Peking Opera performance. That was nine years ago. And in those nine years, the world has changed dramatically. US-China relations, even more so — going through trade wars, tech wars, and a full-blown geopolitical rivalry.
This trip is tight: just three days, two nights. Trump arrives in Beijing on the evening of the 13th, meets with Xi Jinping on the 14th, and flies back on the 15th. Short and to the point.
Sources say the meeting was originally supposed to center on trade — but Iran has recently pushed its way to the top of the agenda. The US wants China to use its leverage over Iran, while China wants to use this moment to push Washington for a clearer stance on Taiwan. So the question is: how much is each side actually going to get out of this?
There are three things worth paying attention to on this trip.
Number one: the CEO list. When Trump visited China in 2017, he brought 29 top business executives with him and signed letters of intent worth $250 billion. This time? The White House and Treasury put together a much smaller list — around 12 companies. Clearly, the focus this time is on managing trade, not hyping it up. And that significantly shorter CEO list quietly pokes a hole in Beijing's preferred narrative — that American businesses simply can't afford to leave China.
Number two: the venue. China has apparently arranged a special centrepiece for Trump on the afternoon of May 14th: a joint visit to the Temple of Heaven.
This is not just some random tourist stop. Think back to 2017 — Xi Jinping arranged an exclusive, after-hours private tour of the Forbidden City for Trump. In Chinese tradition, the Forbidden City is the emperor's home. Inviting a foreign leader there sends a very specific message: "I am the host, and I'm welcoming you into my inner court as a most honoured personal guest." It's designed to build a sense of personal closeness between the two leaders.
So what's the Temple of Heaven all about?
The Temple of Heaven is where the emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties came to perform sacred rituals — offering sacrifices to heaven and praying for good harvests. It was holy ground, the place where the "Son of Heaven" — the one and only earthly representative of the divine — communicated with the gods.
In ancient Chinese political philosophy, only the Son of Heaven had the standing to be there. For anyone else to walk in carelessly was considered a grave omen.
So by bringing Trump to the Temple of Heaven, Beijing has quietly upgraded its symbolic narrative. The message is: "On Chinese soil, everything follows the order we set." And it carries an implicit nod to Xi Jinping's political status as that very Son of Heaven.
But the White House advisors are no fools. Deputy Press Secretary Kelly pushed back with a pointed line when speaking to the media: "Trump never travels just for symbolism." The focus, she said, is on "rebalancing the US-China relationship" — with a priority on "fairness and reciprocity."
What does that mean? Go ahead and play your cultural symbolism games — that's your business. But we're not going to play along with the performance. We're only here to talk about real deals on the table.
Number three: the disappearance of "spouse diplomacy."
Cast your mind back to Trump's first China visit in 2017. First Lady Melania had her own moments in the spotlight. Peng Liyuan personally took her to a Beijing primary school, where they watched a cultural performance and tried their hand at calligraphy. Melania also made her own visit to the Mutianyu section of the Great Wall, received an official "Hero Certificate," and even fed the pandas at Beijing Zoo. Chinese state media covered all of it extensively — framing this warm "spouse diplomacy" as a perfect showcase of China's soft power and a symbol of US-China friendship in full bloom.
So what about this time? According to the current itinerary released by both the White House and China's Foreign Ministry, Melania is simply accompanying Trump throughout the entire trip. No Great Wall. No pandas. No separate parallel schedule. No one-on-one interaction with Peng Liyuan whatsoever.
Commentator Jiang Feng suggests there are actually two very subtle possibilities hiding behind this.
The first: the White House simply has no interest in playing along with Beijing's warm, feel-good "spouse diplomacy" routine — and has no intention of handing China's propaganda machine any feel-good footage it could use to paint a picture of ever-blooming US-China friendship.
The second possibility is even more interesting: Beijing itself may not want to arrange a separate schedule for Peng Liyuan either.
In previous episodes, we've analyzed this more than once — don't be fooled by Xi Jinping's outward appearance of being firmly in control. In reality, after a turbulent few years, his grip on absolute power within the Party has been seriously weakened. There are undercurrents churning beneath the surface, and on many matters, he's no longer the one calling the shots.
Take a close look: how long has it been since Peng Liyuan had a prominent public appearance on the international stage? The last time was May 2024, when she accompanied Xi to France.
Her public appearances in a foreign diplomatic context have since become heavily guarded and restricted — especially after Zhang Youxia, who was firmly opposed to "spousal interference in politics," particularly military and political affairs, ran into trouble, sharpening factional tensions at the top. And especially after Ma Xingrui — the key figure in Peng Liyuan's inner circle — came under investigation.
It's very likely that the Party's internal factions have quietly reached some kind of equilibrium this time around: keep Peng Liyuan off the stage, don't let her conduct independent diplomatic activities, don't give her any exposure that could trigger a fresh political crisis.
Whether it was the American side that proactively cut the program, or Beijing's own internal factions keeping each other in check — if Trump and Xi stand together in front of the cameras, with Melania at Trump's side but no Peng Liyuan next to Xi, that wouldn't just be a diplomatic nightmare. It would be a glaring signal that something is very wrong at the very top of the Chinese Communist Party.
So Jiang Feng's view is that Peng Liyuan appearing in the frame is still the most likely outcome. She'll probably show up — but an arrangement where they simply hold hands for a photo op with no real substantive schedule of her own is itself a telling sign of the quiet power struggle playing out between the US and China. And it's also a reflection of something that can never be openly acknowledged: a weakening grip on power, and a deeply unstable situation behind the red walls of Zhongnanhai.
So what does Trump most want to walk away with from this meeting?
At the top of the list, without question, is Iran.
Trump is coming in part to look Xi Jinping directly in the eye and say: stop playing games behind my back.
China has long been Iran's biggest oil buyer. Even under heavy US sanctions, independent Chinese refineries — particularly the small private refiners concentrated in Shandong province — have kept quietly snapping up cheap Iranian crude at massive volumes. That's essentially a steady blood transfusion keeping Iran's war machine alive.
And it doesn't stop there. Multiple intelligence sources indicate that Beijing has also been quietly providing Iran with military technical support — and even allowing Iranian vessels docked at Chinese ports, including the previously mentioned Gaolan port in Zhuhai, to load up on key chemicals used in the production of solid rocket fuel.
Right before Trump's departure, on May 8th, the State Department and Treasury made a surprise move — sanctioning three Chinese commercial satellite companies, accusing them of providing Iran with satellite imagery to help identify and strike US military targets across the Middle East.
Trump also dropped a hard warning: if China is caught supplying Iran with air defense missiles, he'll slap on an additional 50% in tariffs, just like that.
So Trump isn't coming to listen to Beijing talk peace. He's coming to deliver an ultimatum: either help me put out the fire in the Middle East, or brace yourself for devastating secondary sanctions.
Beyond Iran, what else does Trump want? Real economic wins, of course.
Boeing has been waiting nearly a decade for this moment. New CEO Ortberg is personally traveling with the delegation, hoping to lock in a blockbuster order from Beijing — potentially hundreds of 737 MAX jets and wide-body aircraft.
Then there are the soybean farmers across America's Midwestern states, all watching and waiting for Trump to bring home a big Chinese purchase commitment.
And rare earth supply chain stability is another major priority for the US side. Trump needs assurance that China won't casually weaponize its rare earth export controls to choke off America's high-tech industries whenever it feels like it.
So what does Xi Jinping want in return?
Beijing's biggest headache right now is the ever-growing stack of US export controls targeting China's tech sector — especially advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment used in AI research. If Trump doesn't ease up on these, Xi's much-hyped vision of "new quality productive forces" is going nowhere. On top of that, with Trump's tariff stick always within reach, Beijing is also desperately keen to hold on to the current trade truce.
Then there's Taiwan — a topic Beijing can never avoid. Just on the eve of this summit, Taiwan's Legislative Yuan passed a significantly cut-down special defense budget, which left Washington somewhat disappointed. Beijing will almost certainly see that as a win and use it as leverage — pushing Trump to pull back on arms sales to Taiwan and political support, and maybe even fantasizing that Trump will shift his language from "we don't support Taiwan independence" to "we oppose Taiwan independence."
But based on signals already put out by US officials, Washington has no intention of changing its Taiwan policy. On this one, Xi Jinping is most likely just going to be talking to himself.
We'll be watching closely as the details of this meeting unfold — stay tuned.
But first, let's turn to another piece of breaking news that the US dropped right before this pivotal summit.
The China Eastern Airlines Crash: "100 Million Yuan for 132 Lives"? [ko cần đọc dòng này]
The crash of China Eastern Airlines flight MU5735 sent shockwaves both inside and outside China. Recently, flight data released by the United States revealed that at the moment of the crash, someone in the cockpit deliberately shut off the engines — killing all 132 people on board. And now an even more explosive claim has surfaced: that someone paid the co-pilot 100 million yuan to do it — with alleged ties to a complex factional power struggle behind the scenes.
On March 21st, 2022, flight MU5735 was en route from Kunming to Guangzhou when it suddenly plunged into a mountainous area in Wuzhou at high speed. All 123 passengers and 9 crew members perished. It became one of the deadliest aviation disasters China had seen in decades. To this day, China's Civil Aviation Administration has still not released a final investigation report on the cause of the crash.
Recently, the US National Transportation Safety Board — the NTSB — published key black box data from the crash online, bringing the case back into the spotlight.
The flight data recorder showed that while the aircraft was cruising steadily at around 8,870 meters, a series of puzzling inputs occurred. The plane was switched from autopilot to manual control. The fuel supply switches were manually cut off. And the co-pilot's control column was pushed forward with a force of roughly 36 kilograms.
Within just two to three seconds, the aircraft went from level flight to a near-vertical nosedive. Cutting off the fuel supply robbed the plane of all power. Taken together, the data strongly suggests someone deliberately flew the aircraft into the ground.
According to the Epoch Times, Jeff Guzzetti — a veteran crash investigator who has worked for both the NTSB and the FAA — said the flight data indicates a struggle took place in the cockpit, and that this was likely a case of pilot suicide.
That conclusion lines up strikingly with rumors that had already been circulating online — pointing to co-pilot Zhang Zhengping as the one who executed the fatal dive.
Before the flight, Zhang reportedly left a suicide note at his hotel. In it, he accused China Eastern Airlines of treating him unfairly following its merger with Yunnan Airlines. At 59 years old, he had once held the highest seniority status as a veteran pilot — but had been demoted to the role of co-pilot. He also wrote about losing everything he'd invested in Evergrande's financial products, saying it had left him with nothing to live for. The note also reportedly included criticism of Xi Jinping for driving China's economy into the ground.
After the crash, China's Civil Aviation Administration pushed back, insisting the crew all held valid licenses, had adequate rest before the flight, and passed their health checks on the day — flatly denying the "pilot suicide" narrative.
At the time, police sealed off the crash site while Chinese authorities imposed tight controls on victims' families, journalists, and the media. That response only deepened public suspicion that this was no ordinary accident.
Veteran media commentator Jiang Feng has weighed in on what may have driven Zhang Zhengping to do it. Why would he take 132 strangers down with him? A shocking claim has recently emerged: that as Zhang was spiraling into a mental breakdown, someone offered him 100 million yuan to push that control column — and promised to take care of his family and children after he was gone. And so he pushed it.
As Jiang Feng put it: "The truly terrifying thing here isn't the 100 million yuan. It's the logic of the kill: first, drive a man to the edge of despair. Then offer his family a way out. And finally, turn an entire plane full of people into collateral damage in a power struggle playing out behind closed walls."
So why did this alleged plan emerge in 2022 specifically?
Because on the eve of the 20th Party Congress, whoever was engineering a total takeover of power had set their sights on one of China's most lucrative prize assets at the time — the aviation sector. That sector was a web of vested interests, firmly in the grip of the Zeng Qinghong family network. China Eastern Airlines, headquartered in Shanghai, had long been tied to the hidden interests of the Jiang faction. Xi's camp wanted control of it. But why not just send in the discipline commission for a direct audit? Because going through proper channels meant two rounds of meetings and more than ten months of process.
The rumor goes like this: a powerful force in Beijing allegedly paid at least one pilot a 100 million yuan bonus to sacrifice himself along with that Boeing jet — using 132 lives as the price to completely shatter the Zeng family's grip over China Eastern Airlines. And sure enough, within months of MU5735, Liu Shaoyong stepped down as Chairman. On August 12th, 2022, Liu Shaoyong resigned as Chairman and Director of China Eastern Airlines, citing "personal reasons."
As for why he wasn't arrested immediately — commentator Jiang Feng's read is that the 20th Party Congress hadn't happened yet, and what Xi Jinping needed most at that moment was a smooth re-election. If the China Eastern case had been openly investigated as an act of deliberate sabotage rooted in internal power struggles, the fallout wouldn't have stopped at Liu Shaoyong. It would have dragged in the Civil Aviation Administration, China Eastern itself, the police, and the entire chain of people who handled the black box data — throwing everything into chaos right before the Party Congress.
So after Liu stepped down, China Eastern didn't immediately install a visible Xi loyalist. Instead, the airline's veteran insider Li Yangmin was brought in as acting chairman to stabilize things. It wasn't until October 2023 that Wang Zhiqing was transferred in to serve as both Chairman and Party Secretary of the group.
On June 28th, 2025, Liu Shaoyong was officially announced as being under investigation by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Supervisory Commission. Then on January 4th, 2026, a formal notice listed his charges — project contracting, flight management, and aircraft leasing. But according to Jiang Feng, that's just the surface. The real focus isn't about money.
Whatever happened inside China Eastern Airlines in the immediate aftermath of that crash — Liu Shaoyong knows. Why did the victims' families receive compensation but never a full explanation? Those questions all lead back to him.
Jiang Feng's analysis is that it wasn't until 2025, when the Hu-Wen faction consolidated power, that they had the ability to go after Liu Shaoyong. Their suspicion is that the MU5735 crash was used as a tool by Xi's camp to seize control of China Eastern and Shanghai's broader aviation network. So they arrested Liu to find out exactly what happened during that disaster — and whether he had cooperated with Xi's people to cover it up.
Which raises the question: why is the truth surfacing now?
Back in January of this year, a Chinese male citizen suddenly filed a Freedom of Information Act request with the US government. And he was laser-precise about it. Case number: DCA22WA102. He sent it directly to the NTSB, requesting all documents related to the crash. Jiang Feng says this move is "anything but simple" — because even if an ordinary person knew the US had a Freedom of Information Act, they'd be unlikely to know how to file one, let alone which agency to approach, let alone know the exact accident case number to cite.
If a victim's family member wanted answers, why not file back in 2022? Why wait until January 2026 to go to the United States with this request?
And the timing gets even more suspicious. The documents started exploding across the internet in early May — right when Xi Jinping was in Shanghai. He had been trying to build bridges and stabilize the situation, and at that exact moment, the China Eastern flight data got dropped online. It was as if someone waited for the precise moment he was most vulnerable, then threw it right in his face.
What this person did after getting hold of the documents was also highly unusual. He uploaded everything directly to GitHub and Wikipedia — available for the entire world to download. Then, once the upload was complete, he deleted his own original GitHub repository. Almost immediately, an anonymous mirror appeared, with a note specifically saying: "To protect the privacy of the original uploader, only the document content is preserved. Do not retain any trace of who first uploaded this." The whole sequence was executed with remarkable precision. An ordinary person would struggle to think that carefully and cover their tracks that thoroughly.
Jiang Feng's take: we can't say for certain which faction this person belongs to. But what is certain is that this does not look like a spontaneous, off-the-cuff operation.
The moment these documents surfaced, the questions Xi Jinping fears most came roaring back. Who reviewed this flight data back then? Who decided the full truth wouldn't be released to the public? Who ordered the media to stop asking questions? Who allowed the victims' families to receive payouts but never a complete explanation? Once those questions are out in the open, Liu Shaoyong can no longer be tried as a simple corruption case. What did he report to his superiors? What did his superiors instruct him to do? Did Xi Jinping's people intervene to take down the Zeng Qinghong faction?
And around the same time all of this was unfolding, Jiang Feng points out that some very strange things have been happening in the skies over China.
During the May Day holiday, reports emerged that near the South Third Ring Road in Beijing, a military helicopter that had been circling in the air was shot down — blown apart mid-flight. On board were Xi Jinping's confidential secretary, personnel from the Central Security Bureau, and members of the People's Armed Police.
According to the rumor, these individuals were carrying urgent orders from Shanghai back to Beijing — heading back to hold down the fort for Xi. But they never made it to Zhongnanhai. The helicopter went down on the outskirts of Beijing.
On the same day, a China Eastern Airlines flight from Beijing to Shanghai, after landing at Hongqiao Airport, failed to slow down during taxi and crashed directly into a passenger boarding bridge. Authorities called it a mechanical failure, saying the cause was still under investigation. But before long, an even more explosive version of events surfaced outside the firewall.
The story goes that on board was a minister-level confidant Xi Jinping had been expecting — someone carrying highly classified information to Shanghai. He was seriously injured in the collision right there at the airport. The reason: the captain had received a mysterious phone call, someone who "jumped into the cockpit," and then the plane was deliberately steered into the jet bridge.
These incidents, Jiang Feng argues, are not isolated accidents. They are warning shots — signals sent by the opposing faction to Xi, in the wake of the old China Eastern affair. Xi had gone to Shanghai seemingly ready to go on the offensive. But he found that he could no longer command the guns. To maintain security in Shanghai, he had no choice but to rely on the cooperation of the local Armed Police — and word is that the Shanghai Armed Police flatly refused to provide serious protection for Xi. Cutting corners on protocol, ignoring documents, not picking up calls. Orders went down and nobody followed them.
Ever since the incident involving Li Keqiang in Shanghai, the Shanghai Armed Police commander Chen Yuan — who had once done Xi's faction's dirty work — was quietly shuffled sideways to the Beijing Armed Police at the same rank after the fallout. So Xi Jinping, while in Shanghai, had lost a significant pillar of support.
Jiang Feng also reveals: there are now reports that inside Shanghai's municipal Party Standing Committee, a number of senior officials have been taken in for questioning — including the Secretary-General of the municipal Party committee, figures within the Armed Police system, and even Shanghai Party Secretary Chen Jining himself. Why does the Shanghai chessboard matter so much? Who is protecting whom? Who is defying whose orders? Who is feeding intelligence to Zeng Qinghong? Who left a back door open for Beijing? All of it is now being combed through.
What's happening across the Jiangnan political landscape is no longer a routine personnel shakeup. It's a powder keg about to blow.
And in the middle of all this chaos, another equally seismic event has taken place.
The Fireworks Factory Explosion That Shook China: 1,000 Dead? [ko cần đọc dòng này]
At just after 4 PM on May 4th, a catastrophic explosion tore through the factory of Huasheng Fireworks Company in Liuyang City, Hunan Province.
A massive mushroom cloud rose over the site. Officially, authorities reported 37 dead, 1 missing, and 51 hospitalized. But according to independent grassroots investigations, the actual death toll surpassed one thousand.
About seven or eight hours after the explosion — at 12:17 AM on the night of May 4th — Xi Jinping personally issued his first directive. Then, early the next morning at 6:05 AM, he issued a second. Two top-level orders in a single night.
Now, we all know that in the Chinese Communist Party's system, major incidents are nothing new. Mine collapses, floods, earthquakes, disease outbreaks — they happen every year, some months more than once. But Xi Jinping, still awake past midnight, urgently issuing directives — then issuing more the moment dawn broke? That kind of response is extraordinarily rare in the CCP's entire history of disaster management. If the death toll was really just 37 people, could that truly keep the CCP's supreme leader — a man who has never lost sleep over ordinary lives — up all night?
The truth is, what Beijing is hiding in this incident goes far beyond just the death count.
The company involved is called Huasheng Fireworks Manufacturing and Display Co., Ltd., located in Guandu Township, Liuyang City. The factory covers roughly 800 mu — the equivalent of about 75 standard football pitches.
State media described the blast zone as having "more than ten workshops completely leveled." Nearby residential homes had their roofs blown off and walls collapsed. Buildings 500 meters from the epicenter had every window shattered, with aluminum alloy window frames twisted and warped beyond recognition. CCTV drone footage made it even more staggering: across nearly the entire 800 mu site, almost nothing remained standing — not a single intact wall in sight.
Worth noting: the explosion happened right in the middle of the May Day holiday — but the factory hadn't stopped. They were racing to fulfill an export order.
And there's one more detail that hasn't gotten much attention: the official surveillance system had no footage whatsoever from the critical moment the explosion occurred.
According to a report by China National Radio, the video surveillance room for Liuyang's fireworks industry is housed inside the city's Emergency Management Bureau — but the surveillance footage from the day of the explosion was said to have "no cloud storage capability," because "the fireworks factory lost power, so the monitoring room received no data."
What makes it even stranger is that this surveillance platform was apparently "at a technological level from more than ten years ago," and inspections were only conducted on a random basis roughly once every three months. Yet at the single most critical moment, it captured absolutely nothing. Coincidence — or something more deliberate?
Independent content creator Hu Liren commissioned a friend in the Changsha business community to conduct an on-the-ground investigation. This friend was a former entrepreneur with an extensive local network.
While the site remained sealed off, he gathered firsthand information through outside channels — local officials, industry professionals, and multiple other sources. After receiving this material, Hu Liren went through each data point himself, cross-referencing and verifying it online before making anything public. His conclusion: the actual death toll from this explosion exceeded one thousand people.
Why?
Hu Liren's friend found that the Liuyang area currently has more than 430 registered fireworks manufacturing companies, employing a workforce of over 300,000 people. Hu Liren later found the same figures in publicly available documents — the two sources matched exactly.
300,000 workers divided across 430 companies works out to an average of roughly 700 to 800 employees per factory.
The Huasheng fireworks complex where the explosion occurred spans 800 mu — making it a mid-to-large-sized operation by local standards. Locals told Hu Liren's friend that under normal operating conditions, at least a thousand people would be working inside that factory at any given time.
On top of that, fireworks manufacturing is an extremely labor-intensive industry — not an automated assembly line. It's work that requires workers to hand-pack explosive powder piece by piece, which means it demands a very large workforce.
And at the time of the accident, the factory was running at full capacity.
Put all three factors together: 430-plus companies, 300,000 workers, averaging 700 to 800 per factory — this was a mid-to-large plant that already had over a thousand workers under normal conditions — and it was the May Day holiday, with everyone pulling extra shifts at maximum output.
So you tell me — is it even remotely possible that only 37 people were inside that factory when the explosion hit?
Hu Liren consulted a panel of experts to run a scientific calculation of the explosion's yield. Their conclusion: the blast was equivalent to roughly one thousand tons of TNT.
For context — the atomic bomb the United States dropped on Hiroshima during World War II had a yield of around 15,000 tons of TNT. In other words, the Liuyang explosion was roughly one-fifteenth to one-twentieth the power of the Hiroshima bomb.
An explosion of that magnitude, across an 800-mu site, leveled more than 30 buildings of various sizes — not just "more than ten workshops" as officially claimed.
In fact, CCTV itself interviewed a survivor named Hu Zhengzhang. He said the factory hadn't taken the May Day holiday off. That day, he happened to have called in sick and was getting a haircut at a barbershop about one kilometer from the factory.
The shockwave from the explosion shattered every window and door in the barbershop. Flying glass cut his head.
And that was at one kilometer away. So you tell me — what chance of survival did anyone inside that factory have?
After pulling all of this data together, Hu Liren concluded that the death toll exceeded one thousand people.
One detail that corroborates this: a netizen claiming to be a local firefighter revealed online that on the very first day alone, 26 bodies were recovered — all burned beyond recognition. He wrote: "There were at least one or two hundred people working inside. Plus a small village nearby was completely flattened. Combined, the number couldn't be less than 450."
If only 37 people died, why was such an enormous force deployed to seal off the scene? Why did the country's top leader feel compelled to issue two urgent directives in the middle of the night?
And that brings us to a question that can no longer be avoided. Several analysts in the military and explosives fields have raised serious doubts about the nature of this explosion — was it really just an ordinary fireworks accident?
Jiang Feng, an overseas-based independent commentator who graduated from a military academy and has done extensive research in the military field, converted the blast using military standards and estimated the yield was equivalent to simultaneously detonating somewhere between 30 and 50 tons of military-grade TNT. He noted that the heavy aerial bombs Russia uses to destroy fortified positions in Ukraine carry only a few hundred kilograms of explosive each — meaning the Liuyang blast was equivalent to setting off hundreds of those bombs all at once.
He also pointed out something specific in the video footage: the edges of the mushroom cloud had a yellowish-brown tint. A conventional black powder explosion should produce white or dark gray smoke.
In the military-industrial world, yellowish-brown is the signature color of high-energy military explosives — like RDX or C4.
RDX — also known as "cyclonite" — is the core high-energy explosive component in C4 plastic explosive. C4 itself is made by taking RDX as the primary ingredient and blending it with binding agents and plasticizers to create a malleable, putty-like explosive.
Ordinary civilian fireworks factories use black powder. Military-grade high explosives are a completely different category — with detonation velocities of 6,000 to 8,000 meters per second, capable of raising temperatures at the blast center to thousands of degrees in an instant, vaporizing human bodies entirely. The two are not even in the same league.
Jiang Feng also raised another point: the CCP assigns the public security system — under Wang Xiaohong — to oversee the management of special explosive materials and hazardous goods. In other words, if military-grade explosives were indeed present at that site, they would fall squarely within his jurisdiction.
It's important to stress that the analysis above regarding the nature of the explosives remains in the realm of speculation and multi-source assessment — it has not been officially confirmed. But the existence of these red flags makes the full picture of this incident considerably more complicated.


What do you make of all these developments? Drop your thoughts in the comments below. Thank you for watching, and we'll see you in the next episode.
